question: What primary role does a nurse play in preventing drug errors?

options.A: Manufacturing pharmaceutical drugs in the hospital pharmacy
options.C: Acting as the final safeguard before drug administration
options.D: Prescribing the correct dosage for patients

explanation: The nurse checks the medication order and patient identity right before administration, serving as the last defense against a potential error. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h1)

question: System failures in medication safety usually involve which of the following?

options.A: Patients refusing to take prescribed medications
options.B: Poor working conditions and confusing drug charts
options.C: Lack of interest from pharmaceutical companies
options.D: Intentional harm caused by the medical staff

explanation: System factors like fatigue, poor lighting, and unclear documentation create environments where human error easily occurs. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h1)

question: When should a nurse document that a medication was given?

options.A: At the end of the entire nursing shift
options.B: Immediately after administering the drug to the patient
options.C: Before drawing up the medication in the treatment room
options.D: Right before waking the patient up for pills

explanation: Immediate documentation prevents accidental double-dosing and ensures an accurate patient record. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h2)

question: Why must a nurse use two unique identifiers to check the right patient?

options.A: To find out the patient's next of kin easily
options.B: To comply with hospital billing department rules
options.C: To check if the patient has health insurance
options.D: To prevent mix-ups between patients with similar names

explanation: Checking two unique identifiers ensures the right treatment reaches the correct person, avoiding common name confusion. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h2)

question: How should high-alert medications like narcotics be stored on the ward?

options.A: Inside a secure double-locked storage unit
options.B: On open shelves for quick nursing access
options.C: Inside the general patient bedside locker
options.D: On top of the medication trolley in a basket

explanation: Double-locking high-alert and controlled substances prevents theft, loss, and unauthorized access. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h3)

question: What is the main reason for using tall-man lettering on drug labels?

options.A: To indicate which drugs require refrigeration
options.B: To highlight medications that are very expensive
options.C: To make the expiry date easier to read from afar
options.D: To distinguish sound-alike and look-alike medication names

explanation: Tall-man lettering uses capital letters to emphasize the differences in similar drug names, reducing dispensing mistakes. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h3)

question: A patient is prescribed digoxin. What must the nurse check before giving this drug?
explanation: Digoxin slows the heart rate, so nurses must check the apical pulse to avoid causing dangerous bradycardia. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of checking patient allergies before drug administration?

options.A: To know how long the patient will stay in the ward
options.B: To prevent severe allergic reactions like anaphylaxis
options.C: To determine the patient's dietary food preferences
options.D: To calculate the correct financial bill for drugs

explanation: Checking known drug allergies protects patients from life-threatening immune responses. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h4)

question: What practice must be avoided when preparing injectable medications?

options.A: Washing hands thoroughly before touching supplies
options.B: Leaving a prepared syringe unlabeled on the tray
options.C: Having a colleague double-check pediatric calculations
options.D: Checking the medication label against the drug chart

explanation: Unlabeled syringes easily lead to administration mix-ups and accidental poisoning. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h5)

question: Why is independent double-checking recommended for high-risk drug calculations?

options.A: To train junior nurses on how to write prescriptions
options.B: To catch mathematical mistakes before the drug is given
options.C: To fulfill a formality required by hospital insurance
options.D: To save time during busy morning ward rounds

explanation: Two people calculating independently drastically reduce the chance of a dosage calculation error reaching the patient. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h5)

question: Which type of tablet must never be crushed before administration?
explanation: Crushing enteric-coated tablets destroys the protective coating meant to prevent stomach irritation or drug breakdown. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h6)

question: Why must the nurse stay at the bedside until oral medications are swallowed?

options.A: To ensure the patient actually takes the prescribed dose
options.B: To chat with the patient about their daily recovery progress
options.C: To collect the empty drug wrapper for recycling
options.D: To wash the water cup immediately after use

explanation: Patients may hide pills or fail to swallow them, leading to ineffective treatment or safety hazards if left behind. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of post-administration monitoring?

options.A: To check for therapeutic effects and adverse drug reactions
options.B: To clean up the medication trolley and empty the bins
options.C: To check if the patient's room temperature is comfortable
options.D: To calculate the total cost of drugs used during the shift

explanation: Monitoring helps nurses see if the drug works properly and catch early signs of side effects. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h7)

question: How soon should a nurse monitor a patient after starting a new intravenous antibiotic?

options.B: Only when the patient rings the bell
options.D: At the end of the 12-hour shift

explanation: Severe allergic reactions often manifest quickly, making close observation during the initial minutes crucial. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h7)

question: What is the immediate priority when a medication error occurs?

options.A: Filling out the official hospital incident forms
options.B: Calling the pharmacy department to replace the drug
options.C: Assessing the patient and ensuring their clinical safety
options.D: Reporting the staff member who made the mistake

explanation: Patient well-being always comes first; staff must check vitals and provide necessary medical interventions immediately. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h8)

question: Why do hospitals use incident reports for medication mistakes?

options.A: To increase the cost of patient hospital bills
options.B: To punish nurses who make careless mistakes
options.C: To identify root causes and prevent future errors
options.D: To reduce the number of working staff on duty

explanation: Incident reports provide data to improve work systems and prevent repeating the same mistakes. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T1#GNS125_U4_T1_h8)
